idiom_name: operator method def +(other) returning a new frozen value object
implementation_notes: In Ruby every operator is a method, so closure is written directly: def +(other) on a value object returns a new instance built from the canonical state, while the mutating relatives (concat, merge!, <<) are the non-closed alternatives and have no place on a domain value. What replaces the classic structure is that operator-method convention plus immutability - Ruby 3.2's Data.define supplies a frozen, value-equal carrier whose initialize can validate the invariant, and older code uses Struct plus freeze or a hand-written class with attr_reader-only access. Because Ruby accepts any method name as an infix operator, the same type can also expose domain-named operations (union, intersect) that read just as naturally; keep the arithmetic symbols for genuinely arithmetic combinations, and define coerce when the type must interoperate with built-in numbers.
code_sketch:
Money = Data.define(:minor, :currency) do
  def initialize(minor:, currency:)                 # validate once, then freeze
    raise ArgumentError, "amount" if minor.negative?
    super
  end

  def +(other)                                      # closed: Money + Money -> Money
    raise ArgumentError, "currency mismatch" unless currency == other.currency
    Money.new(minor: minor + other.minor, currency: currency)
  end
end
pitfalls: freeze is shallow and final: it stops assignment on that object, so a frozen Money holding an Array or Hash field can still be mutated through the contained object - deep-freeze or copy the fields.

Ruby's collection operators mutate by convention (<<, concat, merge!), so mixing them with value objects produces FrozenError at runtime, or silently breaks the invariant if the object was not frozen.

Without a coerce method, expressions such as 2 * money raise TypeError instead of returning Money, because Ruby tries the left operand's method first; implement coerce when the type must mix with built-in numbers.
Operator methods cannot change precedence and are expected to mean what the operator means: redefining + on a class that also includes Comparable invites surprising comparisons.
